data.title: ‘It Makes Sense,’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has been busy building a broader space business that goes well beyond launching rockets. The company’s longer-term ambition is to bring launch services, spacecraft manufacturing and mission capabilities under one roof, creating a more integrated space infrastructure platform.

The proposed acquisition of Iridium might just take that strategy another step forward. Rather than simply adding another satellite business, Rocket Lab will gain an established global communications network with recurring revenues, long-term government and commercial customers, and infrastructure that is already fully operational. That could give Rocket Lab a more diversified revenue base while opening the door to new opportunities in defence, connectivity and other mission-critical applications.

An investor using the pseudonym Petri Dish Reports (PDR) is bullish on Rocket Lab, arguing that the Iridium transaction could accelerate the company’s evolution into a vertically integrated space infrastructure provider. In PDR’s view, the attraction is less about adding another business and more about how the two companies could complement one another.

Promotion

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Iridium operates a global low-Earth-orbit satellite network providing voice, data, tracking and positioning services in locations where terrestrial infrastructure is unavailable. Its network is already generating revenue and has established relationships across government, defence, aviation and industrial markets. It is also expanding into areas such as IoT (Internet of Things) connectivity and direct-to-device communications.

For Rocket Lab, acquiring that infrastructure would provide immediate exposure to a mature communications platform rather than requiring the company to build a constellation from scratch. The transaction therefore adds a recurring, infrastructure-like component to a business that remains heavily associated with launch and spacecraft growth.

PDR sees potential synergies across the combined business. Rocket Lab could supply spacecraft, payloads and mission services to support future upgrades of the Iridium network, while Iridium would provide an established orbital platform and customer base. The combination could also strengthen Rocket Lab’s position in defence, secure communications, positioning, navigation and timing, as well as commercial aviation and other specialized markets.

The financial trade-off is significant, though. Rocket Lab trades at more than 50x EV-to-sales, compared with around 2x for the Industrials sector, a premium that reflects expectations for strong long-term growth. PDR sees considerable execution risk, particularly as Rocket Lab works to bring Neutron, its new reusable medium-lift rocket, into service while simultaneously integrating a large and complex acquisition. Any problems with Neutron’s development, launch schedule or eventual commercial ramp could add to the challenges of absorbing Iridium.

Ultimately, however, PDR views Iridium as potentially important because it changes the composition of Rocket Lab’s growth story. Instead of relying primarily on launches and spacecraft, the company could develop a mix of launch, hardware, mission services and recurring connectivity revenues. If the integration succeeds, that could make Rocket Lab a more diversified space infrastructure business with exposure to several markets rather than a company whose fortunes depend mainly on launch growth.

All told, Petri Dish Reports rates RKLB stock a Buy. (To watch PDR’s track record, click here)

So do most of the Street’s analysts covering this stock. Based on a mix of 14 Buys and 3 Holds, RKLB claims a Strong Buy consensus view. Going by the $109.47 average price target, investors will be pocketing returns of 47% a year from now. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘You Have Been Warned,’ Says Top Investor About AMD Stock
data.description:
The AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) juggernaut picked up steam this week, sending shares to new highs after what has already been an extraordinary run in 2026. The stock is now approaching year-to-date gains of almost 200% and recently crossed the $1 trillion market cap mark.

The latest burst of momentum was helped by excitement around Meta’s Muse AI agent and the possibility that agentic AI could create much greater demand for CPUs alongside GPUs. Reports that AMD could raise prices by about 10% in the fourth quarter have also added to the bullish sentiment.

That surge has now left investors debating whether the company’s valuation has run too far ahead of its business. Investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, argues that AMD’s price now leaves very little room for disappointment.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Drury’s central argument is straightforward: AMD’s business is performing well, but the stock is being priced as though its growth will remain exceptional for years.

Rather than focusing on AMD’s trailing P/E ratio, which can be distorted by the company’s earlier lower margins, the investor looks at projected 2027 earnings. Even assuming profitability continues improving, AMD still trades at around 40 times forward earnings.

That valuation becomes more difficult to justify when compared with peers Nvidia and Broadcom, which trade at about 14.6 times and 18.8 times next year’s expected earnings, respectively. In Q2, AMD’s data-center revenue jumped 107% year over year, an impressive result. But Nvidia’s data-center revenue grew 117%, while Broadcom’s AI semiconductor revenue surged 221%.

For Drury, that is the key problem. AMD is not currently growing faster than its biggest AI-chip rivals, yet the market is assigning it a substantially higher valuation. The investor believes that premium reflects expectations that AMD will capture a significant amount of market share as AI infrastructure expands.

The question is whether those expectations can actually be delivered.

Drury sees two broad possibilities from here. AMD’s valuation could eventually correct sharply if investors decide the growth priced into the shares is unrealistic. Alternatively, the company could continue expanding while the stock produces relatively modest returns as earnings gradually catch up with its valuation.

“I’m not sure which will happen, but I’m fairly confident that AMD’s returns will be a lot lower than Nvidia’s or Broadcom’s over the next few years,” the 5-star investor summed up. “As a result, I think investors should ditch AMD’s shares in favor of those two.” (To watch Drury’s track record, click here)

The Street’s analysts appear to think otherwise. In fact, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 30 Buys and 6 Holds. However, the $648.07 average price target implies shares will stay rangebound for the time being. With this in mind, watch out for either price target hikes or rating downgrades shortly. data.title: Alphabet vs. Tesla: One Mag 7 Stock Is a Winner, the Other Faces Too Many Questions
data.description:
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) are both members of the Magnificent Seven, the group of mega-cap U.S. tech giants that has become a major force in the stock market, but both companies are trying to convince investors that their future extends well beyond the businesses that made them tech giants.

For Alphabet, that means turning its AI infrastructure and in-house chips into major new sources of revenue while defending the search franchise that still drives its advertising empire. Tesla, meanwhile, is pursuing a much broader vision involving autonomous driving, robotics and semiconductor manufacturing alongside its core electric-vehicle business.

That leaves investors weighing some very different questions. How much of Alphabet’s enormous AI spending will translate into future revenue, and can Google maintain its dominance in search as AI reshapes how people find information? For Tesla, the debate centres on vehicle demand, intensifying competition and whether its ambitious new projects can justify the expectations already embedded in its valuation.

Promotion

High conviction TSLA bears now have this Tradr ETF

Investor Bohdan Kucheriavyi has been examining both companies, with the two stocks offering very different sets of opportunities and risks.

Kucheriavyi’s case for Alphabet starts with something that is still relatively underappreciated: Google’s Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs. Until recently, customers primarily accessed the chips through Google Cloud. The company has now started supplying TPU systems directly to selected customers, with the first hardware revenue appearing in the second quarter.

The investor points to Alphabet’s $514 billion cloud backlog as evidence that demand is already being locked in. Anthropic has reportedly agreed to spend around $200 billion over five years on Google Cloud and its chips, while Crux AI, a Google-backed AI infrastructure venture, recently secured $22 billion in bank financing to purchase Google’s TPUs. That financing, Kucheriavyi argues, provides a more concrete indication of demand than forecasts alone.

Google’s traditional search business is another important part of the argument. An Evercore survey found that 78% of respondents still use Google most frequently for search, compared with 70% at the low point in 2024 and early 2025. Alphabet’s Search & Other revenue also increased 17% year over year in Q2. Meanwhile, Google’s AI products are gaining users, with both AI Mode and the Gemini app surpassing 1 billion monthly users.

Kucheriavyi also highlights Alphabet’s expanding infrastructure spending and Waymo’s autonomous-driving operation. The latter has expanded to 14 U.S. cities and is preparing to enter Singapore, while Alphabet continues investing heavily to address constraints on AI computing capacity.

Put all that together and Kucheriavyi considers GOOGL a “solid long-term investment.” To this end, the investor rates the stock a Buy. (To watch Kucheriavyi’s track record, click here)

Tesla’s situation revolves around a different set of issues. The company’s vehicle business is facing pressure from weaker delivery expectations, while higher interest rates could make car financing more expensive. Goldman Sachs recently reduced its third-quarter delivery forecast to 435,000 vehicles, below consensus expectations.

At the same time, Tesla is committing substantial resources to projects outside its traditional auto business. The company and SpaceX have announced an initial $16.8 billion investment in Terafab, a planned semiconductor facility in Texas. The eventual cost could be much higher, although Tesla’s precise financial commitment remains unclear.

Kucheriavyi also questions the timing of such spending. Tesla reported a 1.4% operating margin in the second quarter and negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion, while management expects more than $25 billion of capital expenditure this year.

Then there’s the issue of competition. Chinese automakers, particularly BYD, have gained ground in overseas markets, and the possibility of Chinese manufacturers eventually producing vehicles in the U.S. could change the competitive landscape. Tesla’s upcoming Roadster and Optimus projects offer potential new avenues for growth, but neither currently contributes meaningfully to the company’s core financial results.

Given the stock continues to trade far above Kucheriavyi’s fair value (which is not above $92 per share), the investor rates TSLA stock a Sell.

On the Street GOOGL stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, its $428.88 average price target suggesting shares will gain 25% in the year ahead. Meanwhile, TSLA has a Moderate Buy consensus view, while its $388.85 average target implies modest 12-month upside of 5%. (See GOOGL stock forecast or TSLA stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Far From Done,’ Says Top Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk’s (NASDAQ:SNDK) rise has been a phenomenal story, rewarding savvy investors who spotted the opportunity early. Since being spun off from Western Digital in February 2025, the stock has gained roughly 4,900%, turning what was once a relatively obscure memory name into the S&P 500’s standout performer.

After such an extraordinary rise, it would be easy to assume that all the good news is already priced in. Yet Sandisk’s earnings have undergone a similarly dramatic transformation, suggesting the stock’s gains have been backed by a fundamental improvement in the business.

Investor JR Research, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, believes the market might still be underestimating the company’s runway. His argument centres on a shift in AI workloads that could benefit Sandisk well beyond the initial training boom.

Promotion

Two ETFs to trade SNDK long or short: SNXX & SNDQ

JR points to the growing importance of inference, post-training and reinforcement learning at leading AI companies. Unlike the early stages of the AI buildout, when training dominated infrastructure demand, these newer workloads require AI systems to constantly access and process large amounts of stored information.

That makes storage an important part of the equation. The 5-star investor believes the expansion of enterprise AI agents, followed by the potential acceleration of consumer AI agents, could drive another significant wave of demand for NAND.

Sandisk is also trying to make its business less exposed to the traditional boom-and-bust nature of the memory industry. The company expects newer business-model arrangements to account for around two-thirds of its supply commitments, compared with roughly half today. That should provide greater revenue visibility, while leaving around one-third of its supply exposed to spot pricing and therefore potential upside when NAND prices rise.

JR also sees high-bandwidth flash, or HBF, as another potential source of growth. Sandisk expects to begin sampling the technology in 2027. The economics are still unclear, however, so JR regards HBF as future optionality rather than something that should already be fully reflected in the valuation.

For now, the central question is whether Sandisk can sustain its exceptional profitability. JR notes that Wall Street expects margins to remain resilient, with longer-term agreements offering some protection if memory pricing weakens.

On the valuation front, at roughly 8.5 times earnings, the stock is also trading at a lower multiple than it commanded around its June peak, when the P/E ratio approached 15. JR therefore believes investors are no longer paying a premium simply for explosive growth.

The stock has already delivered an extraordinary return. But according to JR, the underlying AI demand story could mean Sandisk’s ascent is far from over.

Accordingly, JR rates the stock a Buy. (To watch JR Research’s track record, click here)

The Street also take a bullish stance here. The analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy, based on 15 Buys and 2 Holds. At $2,195.29, the average price target implies shares will gain 25% over the one-year timeframe. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Another Sign,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is facing more questions over the scale and execution of its AI infrastructure ambitions after the company invoked a “force majeure” provision tied to Project Jupiter, its huge data center campus in New Mexico.

The notice, reported yesterday, was sent to the project’s developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital, and could allow Oracle to defer certain payments if the facility fails to meet its planned 2028 opening date. The move relates to potential delays in securing power for the site, including problems surrounding the natural gas infrastructure needed to support it. Oracle has stressed that the project remains on schedule and said it remains committed to New Mexico.

That reassurance has not removed the broader concerns surrounding Jupiter, with the shares falling by 3.5% in Thursday’s session. The project is already backed by roughly $18 billion of financing, and those loans were recently quoted at just 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, a sign that lenders and investors are assigning greater risk to the project. Regulatory obstacles and opposition from local residents have added to the uncertainty, particularly around the site’s power supply and environmental impact.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

Investor Johnny Rice, who contributes to The Motley Fool, has been skeptical of Oracle for some time, and the latest development does not fundamentally alter that view. Instead, Rice sees the force majeure notice as another indication of the risks attached to Oracle’s enormous AI infrastructure spending spree.

No doubt, the AI opportunity is substantial. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, the division responsible for much of the company’s AI data center expansion, generated $7.4 billion in revenue last quarter, up 121% year over year. Oracle’s remaining performance obligations have also ballooned to $664 billion, representing a huge amount of contracted business that the company still has to deliver.

The problem, Rice argues, is what it takes to fulfill those commitments. Building AI data centers requires enormous amounts of capital, while Oracle’s free cash flow was negative by $5.4 billion in the latest quarter. The company has therefore had to lean heavily on borrowing and equity issuance to finance its expansion.

Oracle now carries $125 billion of long-term debt, before accounting for the $18 billion in Project Jupiter financing. It also has roughly $288 billion in future data center lease commitments that have yet to begin.

For Rice, that combination is the key issue. Oracle has secured a massive pipeline of AI-related business, but converting those commitments into revenue requires the company to successfully build the infrastructure behind them. Project Jupiter illustrates what can happen when power, permitting, financing and local opposition all become obstacles at once.

“I’ve not been a fan of Oracle stock for a while, so the latest reveal of the force majeure notice doesn’t necessarily change my position, but it does further underscore the risk Oracle has taken on in its bet-the-farm approach to the AI data center boom,” the investor summed up. (To watch Rice’s track record, click here)

Rice might not be a fan of Oracle, but plenty of Street analysts are. Based on 27 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 76%, given the average price target stands at $245.75. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: Micron vs. Intel: One AI Chip Stock Is a Bargain, the Other Is in the No-Go Zone, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) are both benefiting from the AI-driven semiconductor boom, but in very different ways. Micron is positioned around the memory products needed to support expanding AI infrastructure, while Intel is trying to capture more of the demand for CPUs used in increasingly sophisticated AI workloads.

Both stocks have also attracted plenty of attention as investors look for the next beneficiaries of AI spending. Micron is heading into its September 30 earnings report with strong expectations around memory demand, pricing and margins. Intel, meanwhile, has rallied sharply as investors digest the launch and early popularity of Meta Platforms’ Muse AI personal assistant and what it could mean for demand for AI-optimized CPUs.

Against this backdrop, a top investor with the pseudonym The Asian Investor (TAI), sees the two setups very differently.

Promotion

Explore why XOVR invested in Kalshi and how it identifies innovative private companies before they reach the public markets.

The case for Micron starts with the broader AI hardware market. For instance, recently, TSMC reported that August revenue rose 53.3% year over year and 10% from July, pointing to continued strength in demand for AI-related chips and data-center infrastructure.

Micron is also gaining ground in DRAM. Counterpoint data showed its market share reached 24% in the second quarter, two percentage points higher than in the previous quarter. At the same time, HBM remains in tight supply, creating favorable conditions for memory manufacturers as data-center operators continue expanding their AI infrastructure.

TAI believes that environment could support both higher average selling prices and stronger margins for Micron. The company posted a non-GAAP gross margin of 84.9% in its fiscal third quarter and is guiding for roughly 86% in Q4. Earnings expectations are also moving higher, with 26 upward EPS revisions compared with just one downward revision.

The valuation adds another layer to the Micron argument. Despite the stock’s huge gains (up 589% over the past year), Micron trades at only around 7x forward earnings.

TAI believes that low valuation multiple reflects expectations that Micron’s earnings will eventually fall back as they have during previous memory cycles. TAI’s argument is that AI could change that dynamic. Hyperscaler spending, rising HBM requirements and long-term memory commitments could support demand for several years rather than producing the short-lived cycle seen in the past.

As such, heading into earnings, TAI takes a bullish stance. “Micron is likely set for a highly impressive Q4 earnings report where the semiconductor company is set to shine in terms of average selling prices and gross profit margins,” TAI, who ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, said. “I expect improvements in both metrics and believe that the market discounts the potential for a massive EPS beat and strong guidance for the next quarter as well.”

Accordingly, TAI rates the stock a Strong Buy. (To watch The Asian Investor’s track record, click here)

Intel, meanwhile, has been caught up in an AI-fueled rally this past week, jumping by more than 20%, and extending recent gains, as Meta’s Muse AI agent sparked renewed enthusiasm for CPUs.

The excitement makes sense from a product perspective. Muse is designed to perform more demanding tasks than a conventional chatbot, potentially requiring more CPU resources for inference and data orchestration. Intel’s Data Center and AI division is already showing strong growth, with revenue up 59% year over year in the second quarter.

But the market’s enthusiasm has to be weighed against Intel’s valuation. The company trades at roughly 60 times forward earnings, a steep multiple that leaves little room for disappointment. That is particularly notable given that AMD and Nvidia reported much faster revenue growth in their latest quarters, at 50% and 106%, respectively.

That leaves the market placing a substantial premium on the company’s ability to turn the AI and CPU opportunity into sustained earnings growth. At current levels, TAI thinks the investment case makes little sense. “Paying 60x forward earnings for Intel seems excessive, and I would caution investors here about jumping into the fray hoping for the continuation of the current FOMO rally,” the 5-star investor said.

Accordingly, TAI rates INTC stock a Sell.

The Street’s analysts also take differing views of these stocks. Micron has a Strong Buy consensus rating, with the $1,526.75 average price target pointing to 12-month returns of 41%. Intel is rated a Hold, while the shares are expected to show a one-year decline of 8%, given the average target stands at $117.56. (See Micron stock forecast or Intel stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Math Ain’t Mathin’’ Says Investor About SpaceX Stock
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) faces a test today (Thursday, Sept. 24), as another tranche of shares becomes eligible for sale following the expiration of part of its IPO lock-up. Up to roughly 328 million shares are scheduled to be released, although that does not mean all of them will immediately hit the market.

The extent of any selling pressure remains to be seen as the days go by. Regardless, investor Eudaemon Research is focused on a different question: whether SpaceX’s ~$2 trillion valuation can be justified by the enormous investments it is making in Starlink, AI and its launch infrastructure.

Eudaemon had previously argued that SpaceX’s valuation had moved too far ahead of its underlying economics. Since then, one part of that argument has changed: AI demand has grown much faster than expected. However, Eudaemon believes the company’s extraordinary capital requirements remain a major issue.

Promotion

Two ETFs for long or short leverage on SPCX

The key point is that SpaceX is becoming its own biggest customer. During the first half of 2026, it completed 78 launches, but only 17 were for customers. The other 61 were internal launches, primarily supporting businesses such as Starlink. That creates an accounting complication because SpaceX does not recognize revenue when it launches its own satellites. The launch costs are capitalized instead, with the eventual economic benefit appearing elsewhere in the company.

This accounting issue is important when considering SpaceX’s proposed $100 billion Starbase Louisiana facility. SpaceX says the site will eventually support thousands of launches each year, with construction scheduled to begin in 2027 and the first launch targeted for 2029. Eudaemon argues that customer demand alone does not appear sufficient to justify infrastructure on that scale. Much of the capacity is intended for SpaceX’s own businesses.

Starlink provides the obvious example. V3 satellites could dramatically expand network capacity, potentially supporting more subscribers and revenue. But Eudaemon points out that investors cannot clearly see how each additional launch or satellite translates into incremental revenue and profit.

The same issue is emerging with AI. AI revenue has surged, but the segment is consuming huge amounts of capital. In the first half, SpaceX generated $12.51 billion of revenue while spending $28.48 billion on capital expenditure. AI accounted for roughly $23.55 billion of that spending.

For Eudaemon, that creates a major valuation challenge. The investor’s reverse DCF assumes SpaceX will generate $100 billion in revenue in 2027, which is already a very generous starting point. Even with that assumption, revenue would need to grow by roughly 38% a year through 2035, reaching around $1.3 trillion. The model also assumes SpaceX eventually achieves a 25% free-cash-flow margin. In other words, even a generous set of assumptions requires SpaceX to deliver extraordinary growth and eventually generate enormous amounts of cash to justify its current valuation.

“Realistically,” Eudaemon summed up, “I doubt this is possible. It is true that AI has developed faster than I assumed earlier. However, SpaceX generated $7.81 billion in Q2 2026. That means, they need to get average quarterly revenue to about $25 billion in 2027 just to reach my $100 billion starting assumption — more than three times the Q2 level.”

To this end, Eudaemon rates SPCX stock a Sell. (To watch Eudaemon Research’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 2 analysts agree with that thesis, although an additional 26 Buys and 5 Holds all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. Over the next year, the shares are expected to gain 57%, given the average target clocks in at $232.07. (See SPCX stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Price Isn’t Right,’ Says Top Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab’s (NASDAQ:RKLB) planned acquisition of Iridium Communications is taking shape, but investors are going to have to weigh the benefits of the deal against a meaningful increase in the number of shares outstanding.

On September 15, the space company announced that it had fully funded the cash portion of the transaction after raising $1.94 billion through an at-the-market stock offering. Rocket Lab issued roughly 29.3 million new shares at an average price of about $66 each. It also cancelled the $3.6 billion bridge loan it had arranged when the Iridium deal was announced in June.

That means Rocket Lab has chosen dilution over billions of dollars of short-term debt. Investor Daniel Sparks, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, believes that was the more sensible route for a company that is still loss-making, although shareholders are paying for it through a larger share count.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

As of August 5, Rocket Lab had around 598 million common shares outstanding. Against that figure, the new shares represent roughly 5% dilution, or about 4.5% when preferred shares that convert into common stock are included.

The financing covers around two-thirds of the roughly $2.9 billion cash consideration due to Iridium shareholders. Rocket Lab can fund the remainder from its existing cash and short-term investments, which stood at roughly $2.3 billion at the end of June.

Sparks sees that as preferable to taking on the bridge loan. The 364-day facility would have left Rocket Lab needing to refinance billions of dollars relatively quickly. That would have been a significant burden for a company that reported a $49.3 million net loss in its latest quarter.

Iridium will add substantial cash generation to the combined business. It generated around $872 million of revenue and $495 million of OEBITDA in 2025. However, it also has around $1.8 billion of existing debt, which will remain after the acquisition.

Meanwhile, Rocket Lab’s recent growth gives some context for its ability to raise such a large amount of capital. Q2 revenue reached a record $234 million, up 62% year over year, following roughly $200 million in Q1. Management expects another record in Q3, with revenue guided between $250 million and $265 million.

However, the dilution does not end with the stock sale. Iridium shareholders will also get Rocket Lab shares when the transaction closes. Depending on Rocket Lab’s share price, between 25 million and 42 million additional shares could be issued. Combined with the stock already sold, the deal could eventually add around 72 million shares, or as much as 12% to the August 5 share count.

The transaction is not expected to close until mid-2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

For Sparks, Rocket Lab’s decision makes sense, but that does not automatically make the stock attractive. At around $72 a share, the company has a market value of roughly $43 billion, more than 45 times its annualized revenue. “Sure, the financing looks smart,” the 5-star investor summed up. “But my view of the growth stock hasn’t changed. I would avoid buying shares at this price.” (To watch Sparks’ track record, click here)

However, that’s not the stance any of the Street’s analysts currently take. In fact, based on 14 Buys vs. 3 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 49%, given the average price target clocks in at $109.47. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: Broadcom and CoreWeave: One AI Stock Is the Right Play, but Avoid the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) are both heavily involved in the AI game, but they sit in different parts of the industry. Broadcom is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the next phase of the AI buildout, as hyperscalers look beyond Nvidia GPUs and pour billions into custom chips. CoreWeave, meanwhile, is focused on building data centers packed with the GPUs AI companies need to train and run their models.

But while both are benefiting from the AI infrastructure boom, an investor using the moniker The Value Portfolio (TVP) sees very different investment cases, with only one of these names poised to make the most of the opportunity.

Looking at Broadcom, the chip giant’s latest results show just how quickly the business is growing. The company generated $29.6 billion in revenue in its latest quarter, up 86% year over year, while free cash flow reached almost $14 billion. Management expects revenue to rise to $34.8 billion in the next quarter, including almost $22 billion from AI.

Promotion

CWVX: an alternative to margin or options on CRWV

For the 5-star investor, the bigger story is what comes next. Hyperscalers are spending enormous amounts on AI infrastructure, but many are also looking for alternatives to Nvidia’s GPUs. Custom accelerators can give companies more control over costs and performance, and Broadcom is positioned to provide the technology behind many of these projects.

Google is a good example. The company has developed its own AI chips, known as Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), as an alternative to Nvidia’s GPUs. Anthropic, Google and Broadcom have agreed to develop up to 5 GW of TPU capacity, while Meta and other major technology companies are also pursuing custom AI silicon. CEO Hock Tan has projected more than $100 billion in AI revenue for Broadcom in 2027, and TVP believes there is scope for the company to exceed that target as custom silicon takes a larger share of the market.

Broadcom also has major businesses outside AI, including networking, along with a long record of acquisitions. For TVP, that gives the company additional sources of growth and cash generation beyond AI. Put it all together and Broadcom represents a “valuable long-term investment opportunity.”

To this end, The Value Portfolio rates AVGO stock a Strong Buy. (To watch The Value Portfolio’s track record, click here)

CoreWeave has also built an impressive AI infrastructure operation. The company has more than 1.5 GW of active power and around 4.2 GW of contracted capacity, while its revenue backlog has climbed above $100 billion. But turning that backlog into revenue requires enormous amounts of capital. CoreWeave spent $9.4 billion on capital expenditures in its latest quarter and expects to spend roughly $38 billion during 2026.

The financial returns have yet to match that spending. CoreWeave generated $2.6 billion of revenue in the latest quarter, up 112% year over year, but adjusted operating income was only $128 million, giving the company an operating margin of roughly 5%.

Financing adds another challenge. CoreWeave’s latest $2.6 billion loan facility carries a spread of 5.5 percentage points over SOFR, a key U.S. interest-rate benchmark, putting its borrowing cost above 9%. That compares with substantially cheaper financing available to companies such as Google.

TVP also sees a longer-term challenge in CoreWeave’s reliance on Nvidia GPUs. As AI companies become more focused on the cost of running models, custom silicon could become more attractive. Anthropic has committed to Google’s TPU infrastructure through its partnership with Google and Broadcom, while Amazon is developing custom Trainium infrastructure for the company.

CoreWeave’s contracted power remains a valuable asset, and stronger-than-expected AI demand could improve its economics. But TVP argues that the company faces heavy capital requirements, high financing costs and a potentially difficult shift toward custom silicon, while Broadcom is positioned to supply that shift. “Fundamentally,” TVP wrapped up, “the firm has no strong advantages versus its major competitors, which are dramatically larger and wealthier.”

As such, The Value Portfolio gives CRWV stock a Strong Sell rating.

data.title: ‘A No Brainer,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock as Earnings Loom
data.description:
Anyone following the stock market will know that Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has been one of the standout performers this year, with shares up roughly 275% in 2026. Despite that huge gain, the stock is still around 16% below the all-time high it reached in late June. With Micron due to report its latest earnings on Sept. 30, the upcoming results could be an important moment for the stock.

The company has beaten expectations by wide margins in its recent earnings reports, and investor  Keithen Drury, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, expects that trend to continue. In the investor’s view, another strong quarter could give Micron the catalyst it needs to reclaim its previous high and potentially move into new territory.

Micron produces DRAM and NAND memory chips, both of which have become critical to the expansion of AI infrastructure. The surge in AI spending has created a huge increase in demand for memory, while chipmakers have struggled to add production capacity quickly enough. That supply-demand imbalance has pushed memory prices higher, creating a highly favorable environment for Micron.

Promotion

The obvious concern is that memory chips are essentially commodities, meaning the industry has historically been highly cyclical. When supply catches up with demand, prices can fall sharply. Drury believes, however, that the current AI investment cycle could last long enough to make that less of an immediate concern.

Nvidia has forecast that annual AI spending could eventually reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. It also expects the five largest AI hyperscalers to spend around $1.3 trillion in 2027 alone. If that level of spending materializes, the industry will need vast quantities of memory chips for years to come.

Micron expects the current supply constraints to continue beyond 2027, partly because its new manufacturing facilities are not scheduled to begin production until 2027 and 2028. Once that capacity comes online, supply should improve and could put pressure on memory prices. Drury argues that this does not necessarily mean Micron’s profits would collapse, given the scale of AI-related demand expected over the same period.

Meanwhile, Micron’s valuation is “dirt cheap.” The stock currently trades at only about 6.6 times forward earnings, compared with roughly 24 times trailing earnings. That gap reflects the market’s concern that the company’s current earnings surge is temporary.

data.title: ‘It’s a Step Away,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is falling today after reports that the company has invoked “force majeure” over Project Jupiter, a major AI data center in New Mexico. The move is aimed at protecting Oracle from potential costs if the project is delayed and fails to come online as planned in 2028. Shares are down ~6.5% as of writing.

The development adds another layer to the debate around Oracle’s huge AI infrastructure spending, which has already weighed on free cash flow and raised questions about financing and execution.

Nonetheless, Oracle recently delivered one of its strongest quarters in years, with record revenue and a rapidly expanding cloud infrastructure business. The company’s Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO), essentially contracted revenue that has yet to be recognized, have reached $664 billion, while management has also raised its full-year outlook. For investors focused on Oracle’s AI opportunity, the scale of the backlog provides a clearer view of future revenue growth.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

But the counterargument is hard to ignore. Oracle is spending enormous amounts to build the infrastructure needed to meet that demand, leaving free cash flow deeply negative. The question now is whether the company can turn its huge AI backlog into profitable growth without placing too much pressure on its balance sheet.

Investor Yiannis Zourmpanos, who ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, believes the latest results provide evidence that Oracle is making progress on that front. He points first to the $664 billion RPO, which rose 46% year over year and included more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts during the quarter. CFO Hilary Maxson said roughly half of the backlog is expected to turn into revenue over the next 36 months, giving Oracle substantial visibility into future sales.

Another important factor, according to Zourmpanos, is how much of that growth is being funded. A significant portion of the new RPO came from prepaid customers or arrangements in which customers provide their own hardware. That potentially allows Oracle to expand its infrastructure without funding all of the investment itself. Zourmpanos sees this as particularly important after Oracle raised $20 billion through an at-the-market equity offering during the quarter.

Meanwhile, the revenue numbers suggest the demand is already translating into significant growth. Cloud infrastructure revenue surged 121% year over year to $7.4 billion, while total cloud revenue reached $11.6 billion, up 62%. Oracle also deployed 850 MW of AI capacity and more than 300,000 GPUs during the quarter, with GPU utilization reaching 97.9%.

Zourmpanos also points to Oracle’s growing multi-cloud database business. Revenue in that area jumped 353%, while the number of customers rose 180%, suggesting Oracle is expanding beyond simply selling AI infrastructure.

The biggest concern remains cash flow. Oracle spent $28 billion on capital expenditures in Q1, resulting in $5 billion of negative free cash flow despite $23 billion of operating cash flow. Full-year CapEx is expected to reach $90 billion to $95 billion, although customer funding should keep net cash CapEx below $70 billion.

Management has not provided a timeline for when free cash flow will turn positive, while gross margins are also expected to flatten over the next couple of years.

For Zourmpanos, that creates something of a conundrum. Oracle now has exceptional revenue visibility, but far less visibility around margins and cash generation. “If Oracle manages to make the AI buildout profitable, its valuation may look pretty attractive,” the 5-star investor summed up.

However, for now Zourmpanos remains on the sidelines with a Hold (i.e., Neutral) rating. (To watch Zourmpanos’s track record, click here)

data.title: Sandisk vs. SK hynix: One AI Memory Stock Is Undervalued, One’s Valuation Is Deceiving, Says Investor
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) and SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) are both major players in the memory market, but they are exposed to different parts of the cycle. Sandisk is primarily a NAND flash business, supplying storage used across consumer, enterprise and data-center applications. SK hynix has a much larger exposure to DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), putting it at the center of the AI infrastructure boom.

That makes the two stocks an interesting comparison. Both are benefiting from constrained supply and strong pricing, but both also face questions about how long the current environment can last. New capacity is being planned across the industry, while memory prices have started to show signs of moderation. For investors, the key issue is what today’s exceptional margins look like once the cycle becomes less favorable.

Investor Louis Gerard has revisited the two investment cases following a series of important developments.

Promotion

SKHY has a long & short ETF? Explore SKHA & SKHN

For Sandisk, one of the biggest changes is its commitment, alongside Kioxia, to more than $31 billion of investment in Japan through 2032. That includes an $11.3 billion new fab at Kitakami, with production expected to begin in fiscal 2029 or later. Sandisk is required to fund around half of the joint venture’s capital spending when the venture’s own cash flow is insufficient.

The timing is important. Sandisk’s current earnings are being supported by exceptionally strong NAND pricing, but Gerard points to signs that this is already starting to moderate. TrendForce expects contract-price increases to slow substantially from the huge gains seen earlier in the year. Sandisk has also seen consumer revenue fall sharply as prices rose, while data-center revenue surged. At the same time, management expects bit growth to come in below its historical range as customers work through higher inventories.

Gerard also questions how much the company’s reported free cash flow says about the underlying economics. Sandisk’s fabs are operated through joint ventures, meaning much of the capital investment does not appear as conventional CapEx on its books. The company nevertheless retains contractual obligations to help fund that investment. The result is a business that can look unusually cash-generative on headline metrics while carrying substantial future capital commitments. “Valuation metrics appear attractive, but FCF yield and ROIC are overstated due to JV accounting and off-balance-sheet capital intensity,” the investor summed up.

Accordingly, Gerard rates SNDK stock a Sell. (To watch Gerard’s track record, click here)

SK hynix presents a different setup. The company has committed roughly 40 trillion won to a major share buyback and raised its shareholder-return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow. Gerard also points to the company’s large net-cash position, which provides substantial financial flexibility through a memory downturn.

Meanwhile, the company generated record quarterly operating profit of 60.5 trillion won in Q2, while its HBM business remains at the center of the AI opportunity. SK hynix began mass shipments of HBM4 in the second quarter and says its combination of performance, power efficiency, yields and cost competitiveness gives it a strong position as the market moves to the next generation.

There are still important risks. SK hynix remains exposed to memory-price volatility, customer concentration and the HBM cycle. Chinese producer CXMT is also expanding its DRAM capacity, potentially putting pressure on commodity memory prices. SK hynix’s proposed U.S. manufacturing plans could require significant capital, while its ADRs trade at a substantial premium to the Korean-listed shares. Its HBM lead also cannot simply be taken for granted, with Samsung having narrowed the market-share gap during the second quarter.

At the same time, the valuation is appealing. SK hynix trades on a single-digit earnings multiple despite its position in HBM and its strong cash generation. The forward P/E is around 7, while the forward free-cash-flow yield is roughly 10.7%. That means investors are paying relatively little for a business generating substantial cash at a time when AI-related demand remains strong. The valuation also looks modest compared with other semiconductor names, particularly given SK hynix’s exposure to the HBM market.

All that, says the investor, makes SKHY a Buy.

Wall Street’s analysts see no reason to pick between the pair, with both claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. SNDK’s average price target stands at $2,195.29, suggesting shares will gain 23% over the coming months. SKHY is expected to climb 37%, given the average target clocks in at $254.70. Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) could be in line for a much larger opportunity with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) after the agency on Monday began rolling out its AI-powered SMART system at the three major airports serving the Washington, D.C., area. The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system is designed to help the FAA manage air traffic more efficiently by using large amounts of data to identify potential congestion and other problems before they develop.

The rollout marks the first time the FAA has put the technology into live operation in the U.S., and it also highlights the agency’s broader push to modernize its systems with artificial intelligence. The analyst argues that the agency’s modernization effort involves several different vendors and should not be viewed simply as a contest between Palantir and Aviation Systems International (ASI). Since then, the stock has been volatile, with investors appearing concerned that the memory maker will find it difficult to sustain the incredible growth it has experienced amid elevated AI-driven demand.

Yet ahead of the print, BofA’s Vivek Arya, an analyst ranked among the top 2% on Wall Street, keeps a bullish stance on the stock. The key issue is whether Micron can keep gross margins around their current mid-80% range into fiscal 2027. If margins hold up, the analyst believes consensus fiscal 2027 earnings of around $150-$200 per share could remain achievable, representing more than 100% year-over-year growth. That would leave Micron trading at roughly seven times forward earnings, below the approximately 10x multiple the stock has historically been able to sustain.

Arya also sees potential for Micron to restart its buyback program from December 9 onward, when restrictions tied to its CHIPS Act grants are expected to expire. Arya expects Micron to forecast fiscal 2027 capital spending somewhere in the mid-to-high $40 billion range, broadly in line with current Street expectations. That would represent a jump of more than 60% from the prior year, but the analyst points out that more than half of the increase should come from longer-term cleanroom construction rather than immediate production capacity.

Industry checks indicate DRAM average selling prices could have risen 20%-30% sequentially in the calendar third quarter, while NAND pricing was up more than 15%. Arya expects another single-digit increase in the fourth quarter. Hyperscalers have also agreed to pay higher DRAM prices in the first half of fiscal 2027 than in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Still, Arya is not assuming the good times last forever and models memory pricing falling by more than 10% in calendar 2028.

Concerns about lower HBM specifications are also being overplayed, according to Arya. Even if Nvidia launches products requiring less HBM, supply could remain tight, while HBM4 and HBM4e should support strong pricing.

Ultimately, Arya sees the SCAs as a sideshow rather than the main investment thesis. They may smooth the memory cycle, but they cannot eliminate it. “If AI capex remains durable, MU’s earnings power and valuation remain compelling; if AI spending weakens, customer purchases and future capacity additions will both adjust,” the 5-star analyst summed up. “The key question is not whether contracts can smooth the cycle, but whether AI investment remains strong enough to sustain it.”

For AMD, JR believes the biggest issue is whether the company can deliver enough additional growth to justify its valuation. AMD’s management has outlined a roughly $2 trillion total addressable market by 2030, including about $220 billion for servers. But JR argues that simply pointing to the size of the opportunity is no longer enough. AMD needs to show that it can capture a much larger share of it.

AI labs could be particularly important. AMD already has a 2-gigawatt agreement with Anthropic, while the AI company could reach around 10 GW of capacity by 2027. JR sees the possibility of AMD expanding its role with Anthropic as one of the biggest potential catalysts for its data center business. On this front, it has already made significant progress. Data center revenue reached $22.2 billion over the past 12 months, compared with just $7.5 billion two years earlier. Its opportunity in so-called agentic CPUs could add another substantial source of growth.

But JR believes investors need to see more than the existing roadmap. Nvidia remains dominant in AI GPUs, while Broadcom is also competing for business from major AI labs. OpenAI is another prominent customer, although its enormous spending requirements and cash burn could affect how quickly it expands its computing infrastructure.

“At 50x forward earnings, there is a lot for the company to prove while we contend with the execution risks on potential buildout delays or even share losses to the current market leaders right now,” the 5-star investor summed up.

To this end, JR has a Hold (i.e., Neutral) rating for AMD. (To watch JR Research’s track record, click here)

SpaceX is a much more speculative proposition, but JR sees potentially greater long-term optionality. The company is building AI data centers on the ground while developing plans for computing infrastructure in space.

SpaceX is targeting roughly $100 billion in annual recurring revenue for 2026 and wants to become one of the world’s largest AI clouds by deployment capacity. Management has discussed reaching as much as 10 GW of AI capacity by 2027.

That target is far from guaranteed. SpaceX is expected to have only a little over 2 GW of capacity this year, meaning an enormous amount of infrastructure would have to be added. Power availability, hardware deployment and demand from AI customers could all constrain the expansion.

JR nevertheless believes SpaceX’s space-based data center ambitions could become particularly important if electricity and grid capacity become major constraints for terrestrial AI infrastructure.

A crucial piece of that longer-term vision is Starship. Successful orbital flights would give SpaceX a path toward deploying the infrastructure needed to put AI computing in space, potentially opening up an entirely new way to overcome the power and grid constraints facing terrestrial data centers. Nvidia is already a key hardware partner, with SpaceXAI using its technology for terrestrial AI infrastructure and planning to use it in its orbital systems.

So while SpaceX offers much greater uncertainty, it also offers exposure to a potentially much larger AI infrastructure opportunity if its plans for terrestrial and orbital computing are realized. It is more about whether Elon Musk can turn an ambitious vision for AI infrastructure into a business operating on a completely different scale by the end of the decade. JR evidently thinks Musk’s plans will come to fruition. “Unless you intend to bet against Elon Musk, I reckon SPCX is still very early in its bid to supplant the rivals in the AI cloud sphere,” the investor said.

Accordingly, JR rates the stock a Buy.

As for Wall Street’s view of these names, both get decent analyst support. AMD is rated a Strong Buy, although the stock’s big run (up 188% year-to-date) means the $644.62 average price target offers only modest upside of 4%. Meanwhile, SPCX claims a Moderate Buy consensus view, but is expected to generate 12-month returns of 51% based on an average price target of $232.07. (See AMD stock forecast or SPCX stock forecast)

data.title: Archer Aviation vs. Rocket Lab: One Aerospace Stock Is a Buy, the Other Is Not Even Close, Says Investor
data.description:
Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) and Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) are both targeting what could become major markets in the future of flight, but from very different directions.

Archer is developing eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) aircraft for urban air mobility, while Rocket Lab is building a broader space business spanning launch services, satellites and spacecraft components.

That gives investors two very different ways to play aerospace. Archer is still working toward commercial operations with its Midnight aircraft, while Rocket Lab already has a functioning business and a substantial backlog.

Promotion

High conviction ACHR bulls now have this Tradr ETF

Against this backdrop, investor Sarah Appino, who contributes to The Motley Fool, has been taking the measure of both names and comes down strongly in favor of only one.

Looking at Archer, its appeal centers on Midnight and the potential for air taxis to become a new form of urban transportation. The company has made progress with flight testing, including piloted city-to-city flights, and is preparing to participate in the U.S. government’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program later this year. Archer has also expanded its ambitions through its planned acquisition of Boeing’s Wisk Aero, Insitu and SkyGrid businesses. Insitu would add more than $200 million in annual revenue, while the other businesses would bring autonomous-flight and airspace-management technology. Boeing is also set to invest in Archer and become a strategic partner.

The financial picture still reflects an early-stage company, however. Archer reported $5 million of revenue in Q2, while recording a net loss of $263.2 million and burning $156.4 million of cash in operating activities during the quarter. The company ended June with $1.56 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments.

Rocket Lab, on the other hand, is much further ahead. Its Electron rocket has established the company in the launch market, while its space-systems business supplies spacecraft and satellite components. Second-quarter revenue reached a record $234 million, up 62% from a year earlier, while backlog climbed to a record $2.36 billion, up 137%.

The company is also working on its larger Neutron rocket, which could significantly expand its addressable market. Rocket Lab secured more than $437 million in new launch contracts during Q2 and the period immediately afterward, taking its launch backlog above 90 missions. It has also agreed to acquire Iridium Communications, a deal that would move the company further into satellite communications if completed.

The risks are different, too. Archer still faces the challenge of obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals and proving it can manufacture and operate its aircraft at scale. It is also taking on execution risk as it expands into defense and autonomous aerospace. Rocket Lab, meanwhile, remains exposed to the technical risks of rocket launches and its reliance on government and commercial contracts. The proposed Iridium acquisition also creates financing and integration risks.

Regarding valuation, Rocket Lab is richly valued at around 49 times trailing sales and about 51 times enterprise value to revenue, but it has substantial revenue and a large contracted backlog that provide investors with a clearer picture of its existing operations. Archer, meanwhile, trades at roughly 558 times trailing sales, so its valuation depends much more heavily on expectations for future commercialization of its aircraft and the businesses it is adding.

For Appino, that difference ultimately determines the choice. Archer could have significant upside if eVTOL aircraft become a major form of transportation, and its expansion into defense and autonomous technology adds further potential. But the business remains dependent on successful certification, commercialization and continued investment.

Appino therefore prefers Rocket Lab, and it’s “not a close call.” 

“Rocket Lab is my pick because it is already generating revenue, winning contracts, and building a business that keeps getting larger,” the investor summed up. “If you’re comfortable with early-stage volatility, Rocket Lab is a more tangible foundation than a company still waiting on regulatory approval.” (To watch Appino’s track record, click here)

Wall Street actually likes both these names. Archer claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, while its $11.60 average price target offers 12-month upside of a hefty 17.5%. RKLB’s Strong Buy consensus view is backed by a $109.47 average target, a figure pointing to one-year gains of 54%. (See ACHR stock forecast or RKLB stock forecast)
